title: qadosh
summary: The Hebrew-scripture references present holiness as both a quality of God and a calling for Israel. Leviticus 19 commands the people to be holy because the Lord is holy; Isaiah 6 portrays the Lord’s holiness in a prophetic vision. First Peter 1 later recalls the Levitical command, and Hebrews 12 urges readers to pursue holiness. These texts connect divine character with human conduct while speaking in different languages and genres.
historical_context: The references move from Israel’s instruction in Leviticus and Isaiah’s vision to Christian letters that draw on Israel’s Scriptures. Their textual sequence supports this comparison; the sources do not supply separate lexical research on the Hebrew term.
canonical_context: Leviticus and Isaiah provide the Hebrew-scripture settings for the holiness theme. First Peter explicitly recalls the command to be holy, and Hebrews calls its readers to pursue holiness. The later texts carry the theme forward, but they are not additional examples of the Hebrew word itself.
literary_context: Leviticus commands, Isaiah depicts a vision, and the New Testament letters quote or exhort. The change in form shows how a call grounded in God’s character can function as instruction for communities in different textual settings.
covenantal_significance: The passages present holiness as rooted in God’s identity and expressed in the life of a people. Leviticus addresses Israel; 1 Peter uses its command in exhorting readers; Hebrews speaks of pursuing holiness. Their connection is the scriptural theme, not an assertion that every passage has the same Hebrew form.
canonical_role: This entry gathers Hebrew passages about God’s holiness and Israel’s calling, alongside later texts that take up that call. It helps readers distinguish the Hebrew-scripture term from the broader canonical theme.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce qadosh to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
